#10389. A “quantum bath” puts quantum entanglement on autopilot

Future quantum computers may depend on the ability to connect widely separated modules through distributed entanglement. Until now, creating this kind of connection has generally required active control and repeated measurements. Physicists at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) have now demonstrated a fully autonomous alternative based on a "quantum bath" made from correlated particles of light.

Published in Physical Review X, the experiment provides the first demonstration of a prediction proposed more than 20 years ago. The approach could eventually offer a new foundation for practical quantum technologies.

Entanglement is one of the defining phenomena of quantum physics. It allows particles or systems to share correlations that cannot be explained by classical physics. Creating distributed entanglement between physically separated qubits (quantum bits) could be important for building larger quantum computers and future quantum networks.

Previous attempts to entangle distant qubits have generally followed one of two strategies. One method sends a single, actively controlled photon from one qubit to another. Another has each qubit emit a photon, with the two photons then matched in an effort to generate entanglement.

The second approach was recognized by the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics. However, it still depends on repeated measurements and post-selection, and even then, the process does not always successfully produce entanglement.

PhD student Alejandro Andrés-Juanes and professor Johannes Fink at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) worked with international collaborators to develop a different solution. Their system uses a quantum bath that automatically brings distant qubits into synchronization. In a prototype device, the researchers used a shared source of correlated light particles to entangle two separated qubits, experimentally realizing an idea that had remained theoretical for more than two decades.

Quantum entanglement can take several forms. Continuous-variable entangled states can be produced efficiently and are therefore relatively accessible. They can be compared with a pendulum, whose position and momentum change continuously.

Many useful quantum technologies, however, depend on "discrete-variable" systems. These involve 'all-or-nothing' forms of entanglement that stationary qubits can use. The challenge for the ISTA team was finding a way to connect these readily available continuous forms of entanglement with the discrete forms needed for practical applications.

"In this work, we aimed to overcome this mismatch between the readily available and the practically useful forms of entanglement," says Andrés-Juanes. "By stabilizing the entangled states remotely, our approach is fully autonomous and requires no active control or measurement."

A Quantum Bath Powered by Correlated Light

Maintaining both entanglement and quantum coherence is one of the major difficulties facing quantum computing.

The researchers addressed that problem by making the qubits' surrounding environment itself responsible for producing and stabilizing entanglement.

"In our method, the quantum bath -- meaning the qubits' environment -- is the source of entanglement. It creates a new ground state through a continuous stream of correlated photons," says Fink. "This way, the entangled qubit state is stabilized, even beyond the qubits' own 'lifetime', and remains always available as a resource for further quantum processing. This makes the approach conceptually significant."

Because the entangled state remains available, researchers can access it whenever it is needed. That differs from temporary entanglement, which has to be used during the brief period when it exists.

To couple the qubits with the entangled photon source, the researchers relied on microwave photons. These low-energy light particles are especially useful for manipulating quantum information and are already central to leading superconducting-qubit technology.

Optical photons serve a different role and are commonly used in optics and atomic physics. They may also become important for carrying quantum information between distant quantum computers through fiber optics, an area that the Fink group at ISTA is also investigating.

The researchers needed to confirm that the two qubits were actually synchronized inside the quantum bath. To do that, they used quantum tomography, a technique that reconstructs a quantum system by examining many different 'slices' of its behavior.

"Qubits can be in a superposition of states, but all these states collapse when we measure them, leaving us with a 0 or 1 state," says Andrés-Juanes.

Quantum tomography allowed the researchers to perform measurements lasting only 20-80 nanoseconds and use those observations to investigate the qubits' underlying states. A nanosecond is one billionth of a second.

A 20-Year Prediction Becomes an Experiment

By successfully entangling two isolated qubits through a quantum bath, the ISTA researchers created a proof-of-concept laboratory prototype for the long-standing theoretical proposal.

"We present a relatively simple method that could be scaled up to synchronize multiple distant qubits," says Andrés-Juanes.

The new approach is promising, but it is not yet as efficient as methods that actively control qubit states. "Our method currently transfers about 10% of the bath's available entanglement."

The researchers suggest that one reason the idea took more than two decades to demonstrate is that the original theory was developed under idealized conditions that are difficult to reproduce experimentally.

"Our experiments helped us reveal several factors that may have prevented scientists from designing a functional quantum bath using a single source of correlated photons for distributed entanglement," says Fink.

The prototype developed at ISTA could provide new opportunities for quantum-optics experiments. It may also contribute to efforts to expand quantum processors and ultimately move them closer to fault-tolerant operation.

Materials provided by Institute of Science and Technology Austria. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10386. How to Create Effective Cold Email Sequences That Generate Replies: A Developer's Guide

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Connecting with prospects via cold email isn't always straightforward, particularly when recipients receive dozens of messages every day. Even a relevant email can get lost in a crowded inbox. That's why many B2B companies use cold email sequences to maintain consistent communication and manage follow-ups.

However, creating effective email sequences involves more than writing messages and choosing sending intervals. Developers building or integrating email automation systems must also consider API reliability, message scheduling, data validation, email authentication, security, and workflow monitoring.

A well-designed email sequence combines relevant communication with reliable technical infrastructure. This article explains how to structure cold email sequences and explores the development practices that make automated email workflows more dependable.

A cold email sequence is a planned series of emails sent to prospective customers who have not previously established a direct relationship with the sender. These messages are delivered over a defined period, with each email designed to introduce an offer, provide additional context, address a potential concern, or encourage a response.

For example, a software development company might contact a growing SaaS business to discuss opportunities to improve its application infrastructure. The first email could introduce the company's expertise, the second could explain a relevant technical challenge, and the third could share a useful observation about application performance.

Each message supports the same overall objective while contributing something different.

From a developer's perspective, a cold email sequence can also be understood as an event-driven workflow. Every contact has a sequence state, scheduled messages, and conditions that determine whether the next message should be delivered.

A basic sequence might follow this structure:

This model is useful for developers working on CRM integrations, email platforms, customer engagement systems, and automated business workflows.

The first step is to establish a clear plan before writing any messages. Determine who you want to contact, what problem your offer solves, and what action you want recipients to take.

Start by defining your ideal customer profile, identifying relevant decision-makers, and researching their business needs. Next, select one primary campaign objective, such as generating positive replies, booking qualified meetings, or exploring potential partnerships.

Decide how many emails you will send, what each message will communicate, and how much time will pass between follow-ups. Make sure every email adds value instead of repeating information from previous messages.

For example, a software consultancy targeting B2B SaaS companies might introduce an application performance challenge in the first email, share a practical recommendation in the second, provide a relevant engineering case study in the third, and close the sequence with a polite final follow-up.

Before launching the campaign, review the prospect list, verify contact information, check email authentication, and test the complete sequence.

Developers should also establish technical requirements before implementation:

Define how contact information will be stored and validated.

Determine which events trigger scheduled emails.

Implement conditions that prevent unnecessary follow-ups.

Establish secure API connections between applications.

Record delivery results, failures, and recipient responses.

These considerations help transform a basic email campaign into a maintainable automation workflow.

Every cold email sequence needs a specific objective. Without one, messages may contain several unrelated offers or ask recipients to take different actions.

A SaaS company might want to schedule product demonstrations, while a software consultancy may want to connect with businesses planning infrastructure improvements. A recruitment firm might aim to establish relationships with technical hiring managers.

Your objective should influence the message and call to action.

For developers building campaign dashboards, goals should also be represented through measurable application events.

This example demonstrates how a dashboard might calculate a positive reply rate from stored campaign events.

In production, developers should also handle zero denominators, duplicate events, inconsistent reporting periods, and differences between accepted, delivered, and failed messages.

Effective cold email sequences begin with the right audience. Even a well-written email is unlikely to generate meaningful replies if it reaches people who have no interest in the subject.

Start by defining your ideal customer profile. Consider industry, company size, location, business model, growth stage, and the challenges your product or service addresses.

For example, a development consultancy offering cloud migration assistance might contact CTOs, engineering managers, and technical founders. Although these professionals may benefit from similar services, their priorities can differ.

A CTO may focus on infrastructure reliability and operational costs, while an engineering manager may prioritize deployment workflows, maintainability, and team productivity.

Segment prospects according to meaningful differences rather than sending identical messages to everyone.

Audience segmentation can be implemented through database queries, CRM filters, or API-based contact management.

A simplified contact object might look like this:

Structured data makes segmentation more predictable and helps prevent inconsistent personalization.

Contact data should be collected and processed lawfully, with appropriate access controls and retention policies.

Personalization helps prospects understand why you are contacting them specifically. However, effective personalization involves more than inserting a first name, company name, or job title into a template.

Research relevant professional information that connects the recipient's business to your offer.

For example, a development consultancy contacting a SaaS company could mention a recently announced application launch and explain how scalable deployment practices may support future growth.

The observation should be accurate and connected to a genuine technical challenge.

A practical personalization process involves three steps:

Identify a relevant professional observation.

Explain why it may matter to the recipient.

Connect it naturally to the proposed solution.

Developers can support this process with reusable templates and structured variables.

This simple example demonstrates template personalization.

In production, developers should validate template variables, prevent accidental disclosure of customer data, and escape untrusted values when generating HTML.

The subject line gives recipients an initial indication of what an email contains. A clear, relevant subject line helps them recognize the message's purpose.

Keep subject lines concise and connected to the recipient's business needs. Avoid exaggerated promises, artificial urgency, and misleading claims.

A question about your development workflow

Ideas for improving deployment reliability

A question about your engineering process

The best subject line depends on the audience and purpose.

Developers building email systems should also consider subject-line encoding, Unicode handling, template validation, and protection against header injection.

For example, email libraries should be responsible for constructing message headers rather than applications manually concatenating untrusted header strings.

SitePoint's tutorial on sending email using Node.js provides additional guidance on email construction and delivery.

The first email introduces your business and gives the prospect a reason to consider your offer.

A useful structure includes a personalized opening, a clear value proposition, a brief explanation of relevant expertise, and one simple call to action.

For example, a development consultancy contacting a SaaS business might explain that it helps software teams improve deployment workflows and application reliability.

Avoid introducing every service you offer or listing multiple benefits in the same email.

From a technical perspective, the first message should also establish the recipient's sequence state.

This state information allows a background worker to determine when an email is eligible for delivery.

Before sending, the worker must recheck the latest recipient status. A scheduled job should never override a newly recorded opt-out.

Subject: A question about your development workflow

I noticed [relevant observation about the company's software development process] and thought there might be an opportunity to improve deployment reliability.

Our team works with growing software companies on application infrastructure, development workflows, and performance improvements.

Is improving your development infrastructure a priority for your team this quarter?

The personalized observation should be specific and accurate. A concise message is more useful than a generic introduction filled with broad claims.

An effective cold email sequence follows a logical progression. Each message builds on the initial contact by introducing new information, clarifying value, or offering another way to engage.

Email sequencing tools can help teams schedule messages and manage follow-ups consistently. For developers integrating these systems into existing applications, it is important to understand how scheduling, contact states, reply events, and automation rules interact.

A five-email sequence can provide a practical starting point:

These intervals are starting points rather than universal rules. Adjust them to suit the audience, recipient preferences, and campaign performance.

For developers, scheduling is one of the most important technical aspects of email automation.

Sending messages directly inside an HTTP request can create unnecessary delays and make failure handling difficult.

A more reliable architecture uses background jobs.

This approach separates campaign management from email delivery.

For example, a worker can process scheduled messages independently while the main application continues handling user requests.

SitePoint's guide to implementing a task queue in Node.js explains how background processing can support workloads such as email delivery.

Production implementations should include persistent scheduling, retry policies, rate limiting, and idempotency controls to reduce duplicate messages.

Follow-up emails give prospects another opportunity to respond when they overlook an initial message or need additional information.

Each follow-up should introduce a useful detail, clarify the offer, or address a relevant concern.

For example, a software consultancy could use its first follow-up to explain a common deployment bottleneck. A later message might share a relevant case study or describe how the consultancy approaches application monitoring.

Subject: Re: A question about your development workflow

I wanted to follow up on my previous message.

One area worth reviewing is whether your deployment process includes automated testing, rollback procedures, and application performance monitoring.

These practices can help development teams identify problems earlier and improve release reliability.

Would a brief conversation about your current development workflow be useful?

This follow-up adds context without repeating the original message.

Stop the sequence when someone replies, opts out, or otherwise indicates that further contact is unwelcome.

Prospects receiving unsolicited emails may have little reason to trust an unfamiliar sender.

Relevant evidence helps establish credibility.

Social proof can include verified customer results, technical case studies, industry experience, or examples of previous work.

For example, a software consultancy might share a documented case study showing how automated testing reduced deployment failures.

When case studies are unavailable, demonstrate expertise through a practical observation or useful recommendation.

Developers building campaign systems should ensure that reusable case studies and message templates are versioned appropriately. This makes it easier to identify which content was sent and prevents outdated claims from being reused unintentionally.

Avoid exaggerated claims, invented statistics, and guarantees that cannot be supported.

A call to action tells the recipient what to do next.

In cold email outreach, a complicated request can discourage engagement because the prospect has not yet developed enough interest to commit time or resources.

Is this a priority for your team right now?

Would a short technical overview be useful?

Are you the right person to discuss this with?

Would you be open to exploring a potential partnership?

Choose a CTA that matches the purpose of the email.

Developers designing email templates should also consider accessibility. Links should use descriptive text, buttons should have sufficient contrast, and HTML emails should include readable plain-text alternatives.

Beyond content and scheduling, developers need to ensure that automated email workflows operate securely and consistently.

Email authentication helps receiving systems evaluate whether a message is authorized to use its sending domain.

SPF (Sender Policy Framework): Identifies servers authorized to send mail for a domain.

DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail): Uses cryptographic signatures to help verify message integrity and signing-domain responsibility.

DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance): Defines how SPF or DKIM authentication should align with the visible From domain and provides reporting capabilities.

Developers responsible for email infrastructure should understand how these mechanisms work together.

SitePoint's article on email deliverability provides additional context about authentication, sender reputation, and delivery reliability.

Modern email workflows often integrate CRM systems, databases, automation platforms, and email service providers.

REST APIs allow developers to exchange information between these applications.

For example, an application might synchronize contact records, create campaigns, retrieve reply events, or update sequence states.

When building integrations, developers should:

Avoid exposing sensitive information in logs.

These practices improve maintainability and reduce the risk of inconsistent campaign data.

Webhooks allow external platforms to notify applications when events occur.

A simplified event handler could look like this:

This example illustrates application-level event handling rather than a particular provider's webhook format.

A production webhook endpoint must verify the provider's authentication or signature mechanism before processing events. It should also handle duplicate deliveries, out-of-order events, and temporary database failures.

Testing is essential when an application sends automated messages.

Messages are scheduled at the correct times.

Failed jobs do not create duplicate messages.

Templates render correctly across email clients.

API failures produce useful operational logs.

Tools such as Postman, Mailpit, and automated integration tests can help validate different parts of the workflow.

Use synthetic recipients and controlled test environments rather than sending test campaigns to real prospects.

Developers building campaign dashboards or CRM-connected applications may need to integrate an external sequencing platform rather than implement every sending feature themselves.

EmailBison is one example of a platform for managing cold email campaigns and follow-ups. Its API and integration capabilities make it relevant when evaluating how a third-party email system can fit into an existing application architecture.

For developers, the main consideration is not simply whether a platform can schedule messages, but how its capabilities interact with the application's data model and operational requirements.

For example, a CRM integration might follow this workflow:

This architecture introduces several engineering considerations.

Data synchronization: Contact records must remain consistent between the CRM and the email platform.

Error handling: API failures should be recorded and retried safely when appropriate.

Security: API credentials and contact information should be protected.

Observability: Developers should be able to investigate failed operations without exposing sensitive information.

The same architectural principles apply to other email automation providers. Before choosing an integration, review its current API documentation, authentication model, event coverage, rate limits, and data-handling requirements.

Several common mistakes can reduce the effectiveness and reliability of cold email outreach, even when businesses use automation.

Sending generic messages: Emails that could apply to any business fail to establish relevance. Use appropriate segmentation and accurate personalization.

Repeating the same pitch: Every follow-up should contribute something new instead of repeating the original message.

Making emails too long: Excessive explanations and multiple offers make it harder for prospects to identify the main point.

Using aggressive follow-ups: Sending messages too frequently can frustrate recipients. Choose reasonable intervals and respect recipient preferences.

Making unsupported claims: Exaggerated results and misleading promises damage credibility.

Ignoring recipient responses: Stop automated sequences when someone replies, opts out, or requests no further contact.

Failing to handle duplicate events: A webhook may be delivered more than once. Applications should use idempotent processing to avoid repeated actions.

Ignoring API failures: Temporary provider outages and rate limits should not silently corrupt campaign state.

Insufficient testing: Automation workflows should be validated with controlled test data before production deployment.

Scaling too quickly: Increasing sending volume before validating deliverability, infrastructure, and workflow reliability can amplify existing problems.

Avoiding these mistakes helps teams maintain a professional communication process while reducing operational risks.

A cold email sequence can start with three to five emails, including the initial message and follow-ups. The appropriate number depends on the audience, purpose, and recipient preferences.

Focus on providing useful information rather than increasing the number of messages unnecessarily.

Yes. Developers can integrate email sequencing platforms with web applications through APIs, webhooks, and background workers.

Common use cases include CRM synchronization, campaign dashboards, reply tracking, and workflow automation.

A practical starting point is two to four days before the first follow-up, followed by slightly longer intervals between later messages.

The schedule should account for recipient preferences and stop immediately when further contact is unwanted.

Yes. Sequencing tools can automate scheduling, follow-ups, contact management, and reply detection.

Human oversight remains important for message quality, data accuracy, security, and responding appropriately to interested prospects.

Testing should also verify that automated messages are not sent to suppressed contacts.

Yes. Small businesses may prioritize straightforward communication and immediate practical benefits, while enterprise prospects may require more information about security, integration, scalability, and stakeholder approval.

From a development perspective, enterprise integrations may also require stronger access controls, audit logging, and data synchronization.

Creating effective cold email sequences requires relevant messaging, thoughtful follow-ups, and reliable automation.

For developers, the underlying technical systems are just as important as the messages themselves. Contact validation, background scheduling, API integrations, email authentication, webhook processing, and error handling all contribute to dependable email workflows.

By treating email sequencing as a structured, event-driven application process rather than simply a series of scheduled messages, development teams can build systems that are easier to test, monitor, maintain, and extend.

The goal is not merely to send more emails. It is to create a reliable communication workflow that respects recipients and supports meaningful conversations.

#10385. Scientists just made quantum computer operations 1,000 times faster

Quantum computers remain highly vulnerable to errors and tiny disturbances from their surroundings. The longer a quantum operation takes to complete, the more time there is for those errors to build up. Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have now developed a method that can perform a broad range of advanced quantum operations more than a thousand times faster. The advance tackles a major obstacle in the field and could help move quantum computing closer to becoming fault-tolerant.

Quantum computers could eventually transform areas such as drug discovery, energy technology, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and logistics. Before that can happen, however, these machines need to become much more dependable.

A major challenge is that quantum computations can be disrupted by extremely small environmental effects. Electrical noise, cosmic radiation, and overheating can all introduce errors while information is being processed.

Traditional computers can experience errors too, but decades of development have produced reliable error correction methods that can quickly detect and repair them. Quantum systems are much harder to protect because the information they use is extraordinarily delicate.

"The fundamental building blocks of quantum computers, known as qubits, are so sensitive that even the smallest disturbance can cause the quantum state to deviate from the target, resulting in the loss of information. If too many errors accumulate before they can be corrected, the computation can fail," says Lei Du, researcher in Applied Quantum Physics at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden, and lead author of the theoretical study published in the journal Physical Review Letters.

A Different Way to Protect Quantum Information

To make quantum computing more resilient and eventually fault-tolerant, researchers are investigating new ways to shield quantum information from errors. One promising strategy uses so-called bosonic quantum codes*.

Instead of assigning quantum information to individual qubits, this approach stores it in microwave fields inside superconducting circuits.

"Rather than storing quantum information in individual qubits, bosonic codes encode information in the microwave fields found within superconducting circuits. This approach has been shown to provide stronger protection against certain types of errors," explains Tangyou Huang, researcher in Quantum Technology at Chalmers and co-author of the study.

Quantum Operations More Than 1,000 Times Faster

Working with bosonic quantum codes is not simple. Creating and controlling the required quantum states has traditionally involved guiding a quantum system through thousands of repeated driving cycles.

That process can take considerable time, and every additional cycle creates another opportunity for outside disturbances to interfere with the calculation. In quantum computing, speed is therefore closely tied to reliability.

Chalmers researchers Lei Du and Tangyou Huang have now proposed a different strategy. Rather than constructing the desired quantum states one small piece at a time, their method can perform a wide variety of operations much faster.

"Our method shows that a diverse range of quantum operations on bosonic states can be completed within a single driving cycle, rather than the several thousand cycles that have been required previously. This makes the operations both faster and more efficient, while reducing the risk that disturbances will corrupt the information before the process is finished. It represents an important step towards fault-tolerant quantum computers," says Lei Du.

The new approach is built around Quantum lattice gates, a recently proposed universal set of quantum gates developed by the same research team.

These gates act somewhat like shortcuts. Instead of requiring a long sequence of repeated control steps, they can allow the intended quantum operation to be completed in just one driving cycle. That could make the process faster, simpler, and less vulnerable to errors.

"You can think of it like building a large Lego castle. Instead of assembling it brick by brick and risking mistakes along the way, quantum lattice gates act like pre-built Lego modules that can be connected quickly and efficiently," says Tangyou Huang.

Designed for Superconducting Quantum Computers

The technique is especially well suited to superconducting quantum computers, which are among the most prominent technologies being developed in the international push toward large-scale quantum computing.

Chalmers University of Technology is also using superconducting technology as it develops a 100-qubit quantum computer.

"A key advantage of our approach is that it can be implemented using existing superconducting quantum circuit platforms. We are already discussing possible experimental realizations with colleagues at Chalmers, and we hope to see a demonstration of the method in the near future," says Tangyou Huang.

The researchers say the work addresses a central problem facing the field: efficiently producing and controlling quantum states that are capable of helping correct errors.

"Our results address one of the major bottlenecks in the field: how to quickly and reliably create and control the error-correcting quantum states that could play an important role in future quantum computers," says Lei Du.

More About Bosonic Codes, Quantum Lattice Gates and Floquet Control

*Bosonic quantum codes store quantum information in the states of, for example, microwave or optical resonators rather than in individual qubits. They are considered a promising tool for quantum error correction because they can provide built-in protection against certain types of errors.

Quantum operations are needed to process that stored information. Quantum lattice gates are a recently proposed collection of basic building blocks that can be used to control bosonic quantum states. By combining and designing these gates, researchers can carry out a wide range of more complicated quantum operations.

One method for implementing these operations is known as Floquet control, which uses periodic control signals to drive a quantum system. Earlier Floquet-based techniques have generally depended on slower processes involving many repeated driving cycles. The approach developed at Chalmers can instead perform quantum lattice gates directly in a single driving cycle, making some operations more than a thousand times faster.

The scientific paper "Single-Period Floquet Control of Bosonic Codes with Quantum Lattice Gates" has been published in Physical Review Letters. The authors are Tangyou Huang, Lei Du, and Lingzhen Guo. The researchers are affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden and Tianjin University in China.

The research was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology (WACQT), and the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation.

Materials provided by Chalmers University of Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Plymouth City Council unanimously voted to end its Flock contract in September 2026, but the company failed to respond to demands to remove its cameras installed around the city. According to The Drive, the city informed Flock immediately about the cancelation, but it failed to respond even after a week. Because of this, Plymouth Police Chief Eric Fadden was forced to take matters into the city’s hands and physically disconnected the cameras’ power cords to ensure that they are non-functional.

“As you’re well aware, the City Council voted to discontinue the use of Flock ALPRs at the Sept. 22 meeting. On the morning of Sept. 23, we suspended all Plymouth user Flock accounts and notified Flock Safety of the Council’s decision. We followed up with a formal letter of cancellation via US Mail and email after consulting with our City Attorney’s Office. We did not hear any reply from Flock Safety Corporate or Legal, other than some communication with our local representative,” Fadden told The Drive. “After hearing nothing for more than a week, I directed our staff to disconnect the power cords from the cameras in order to be sure that they are not functioning or recording plates.”

Flock has been hit by multiple controversies in recent months, including the arrest of officers for misusing the system and the mistaken “ambush” of a car reviewer by Plymouth City Police in Minnesota over an administrative error made in California. There have even been reports that police have been pulling motorists over because an AI algorithm deemed their travel history as “suspicious.” Dayton, another city in Minnesota located just 10 miles north of Plymouth, has also paused its Flock program and disabled the two devices in the area. The Dayton police became aware that the company intended to replace these cameras and told Flock not to proceed with the work order. However, it moved forward with the replacement anyway despite being instructed otherwise.

#10380. Tiny nanolaser could cut computer energy use in half

The development of a nanolaser could mark an early step toward a future in which microchips communicate entirely with particles of light.

Researchers at DTU have created a tiny nanolaser that could eventually help make computers, smartphones, and data centers faster while using much less energy. The breakthrough was published in the scientific journalScience Advances.

In the future, thousands of these lasers could potentially be integrated onto a single microchip. Instead of moving information around a chip with electrical signals, devices could transmit data using photons, the particles that make up light.

"The nanolaser opens up the possibility of creating a new generation of components that combine high performance with minimal size. This could be in information technology, for example, where ultra-small and energy-efficient lasers can reduce energy consumption in computers, or in the development of sensors for the healthcare sector, where the nanolaser's extreme light concentration can deliver high-resolution images and ultrasensitive biosensors," says DTU professor Jesper Mørk.

Mørk co-authored the study with, among others, Drs. Meng Xiong and Yi Yu from DTU Electro.

Much of the internet already relies on light to carry information through fiber optic cables. Inside computers, however, data still moves through electronic circuits using electricity. That approach produces heat and can limit how quickly information can be transferred.

Nanolasers could bring optical communication directly onto microchips. By generating light signals efficiently inside the chip, they could allow information to move with very little energy loss, potentially making future devices faster, cooler, and more energy efficient.

Mørk estimates that using nanolasers in computers could reduce energy consumption by as much as half.

The compact DTU nanolaser is an important step toward that goal. Future chips designed around light-based communication would likely require thousands of extremely small, efficient lasers working together to transmit information across the chip.

The new nanolaser was created in DTU's clean room facility, DTU Nanolab. According to Mørk, the device pushes beyond the conventional limit for how small a laser can be made.

At its core is a structure known as a nanocavity, which traps and concentrates light within an exceptionally tiny space. Until now, achieving such intense confinement at this scale had been considered extremely difficult.

When researchers shine a beam of light onto the device, both photons and electrons become concentrated in the same microscopic region. This interaction allows the laser to function at room temperature while requiring unusually little energy.

The light-trapping structure used in the nanolaser was originally developed by Professor Ole Sigmund's group at DTU Construct.

The next major challenge is making the nanolaser operate using electrical power. If researchers can achieve that, the technology could have broad applications across computing, communications, and healthcare.

Computers and smartphones could potentially deliver greater performance while consuming less electricity. Data centers, which require enormous amounts of power, could also see substantial reductions in energy use, potentially leading to significant climate benefits.

In healthcare technology, the nanolaser's ability to concentrate light into an extremely small area could support ultra-sensitive sensors and high-resolution imaging systems.

Researchers estimate that the remaining technical challenges could be solved within the next 5-10 years.

It runs from a USB stick before Windows loads and has to run again on every boot.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new open-source UEFI tool boots from USB and unlocks significant extra tensor performance on RTX 20, 30, and 40-series desktop and laptop GPUs, making the half-speed AI throttle hack a whole lot easier to try on Windows. No VBIOS flash or patched driver needed: the tool runs from a FAT32 stick before the Nvidia driver loads at every boot, and then voila, the developer’s own laptop RTX 4060 hit 65% higher FP16 math.

The “UEFI pre-driver NVIDIA GPU unlocker,” or nv-uefi-unlocker project, removes Nvidia’s tensor limiter using the community V67 payload with read-back verification. This tricks Nvidia’s signed Booter firmware into opening the write lock on two speed-selector registers, allowing the tensor units to run at full rate. The unlock can now run entirely from a bootable USB drive, on Windows as well as Linux, whereas previously it worked primarily through manually installed Linux modules, with Windows support only experimental. The read-back verification part makes things safer, which was a concern with the experimental builds.

The release ships only scripts and self-built binaries, without any Nvidia firmware in the download. Instead, one of the scripts grabs Nvidia’s public 610.43.03 driver packages, verifies them, then rebuilds the firmware files locally. The project credits Zagitta’s gpu-unlock as its porting source and builds on several other community projects, including the RTX 40 fork gpu-unlock-ada and an earlier Windows EFI tool. Having one tool for the many GeForce owners on Windows should significantly open up the hack to a wider audience. Previously, it was scarier-looking, and project progression is rapid these days with AI tools.

The steps right now involve downloading the release, running that script, and then copying the rebuilt files and a BOOTX64.EFI for booting to a FAT32-formatted USB stick. The unlocker can then be run from a one-time boot menu by using the spacebar within 30 seconds for confirmation. Once complete, things are handed off to the respective OS loader.

The unlocker runs in a firmware stage before the OS loads Nvidia’s GPU driver, which means there’s no need to flash the card’s video BIOS or to modify the driver; as the FAQ puts it, the unlock doesn’t “persist through power loss.” The trade-off is running it again on every boot. The system must be booted in UEFI mode with Secure Boot either off or set to trust a self-signed EFI. For a game’s anti-cheat that requires Secure Boot, the tool “CANNOT bypass this requirement,” a developer team member relayed on Reddit. RTX 20 owners have to run a bundled script once to switch the Windows Nvidia driver into GSP firmware mode, before restarting.

Laptop GPUs were already supported by earlier projects, but here one of the developer’s own test cards is a laptop GPU, and laptop results are logged card by card. For laptops, the discrete Nvidia GPU must be powered at entry, which means dGPU-only, or MUX, mode is recommended. On Linux distributions such as Ubuntu, runtime power management can power down the GPU when idle and silently erase the unlock. The English FAQ covers workarounds for this, with instructions and guidelines for other situations.

Compatibility otherwise includes RTX 20-series support listed as “fully compatible; some models have known issues,” while RTX 30-series cards are “fully compatible,” and the tool is “fully compatible on laptops and desktops” using RTX 40-series cards. The GTX 16 is “theoretically compatible” with verification pending, but other cards, including pre-Turing, the GA100, and RTX 50-series cards, are unsupported. The project routes support by chip family, so a card being covered doesn’t mean that specific card has been tested. Cards verified by the tool’s own Windows results are listed in the table below.

RTX 2080, 2080 Ti and 2080 Super fail at boot or handoff; GTX 16 untested; needs GSP firmware mode and a restart first

RTX 3080 (incl. LHR), 3060 Ti, 3060 12GB, 3080 Ti Laptop, 3070 Laptop

RTX 3050 untested; persistence on Thunderbolt eGPUs not guaranteed

RTX 4090, 4080, 4070 Ti Super, 4070 Super, 4070, 4060 Ti 8GB and 16GB, 4060 Laptop, 4050 Laptop

Results compare each card before and after the unlock on the same test, but the tests differ from row to row, so they shouldn’t be compared across cards.

The developer’s own desktop RTX 2070 went from about 34 TFLOPS in FP16 matrix multiply at 8192 to around 62 TFLOPS in the screenshots below.

Some caveats still exist, and Zagitta, whose gpu-unlock kicked off the GeForce unlocks, now says in its FAQ that “I don’t run windows and don’t plan to maintain it,” pointing Windows users to a separate port and warning to be careful with unofficial Windows installers. Results from the unlock are also contingent on power and thermal limits. The new project says it can be combined with the nvoc power-limit unlock, but warns this “can exceed factory power and thermal envelopes.” A per-card ROM hash check, which the project’s own safety rules require, isn’t built yet, and the unlock’s persistence on Thunderbolt eGPUs “is not guaranteed.”

Other cards, including the RTX 2080 and the RTX 2080 Ti, are under review. No dates are promised. The pro-card tensor feature can now be unlocked for many, though, and as simply as using a USB boot drive, which will get even easier with a boot-from-disk toggle the team says is in the works. RTX 50-series owners have to wait, for now, as the team is still trying to crack those cards, which have “a lot more security” than it anticipated.

#10376. How to Organize CSS with Cascade Layers in Large Web Projects

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

As a website grows, its stylesheet often becomes harder to maintain. A rule added to fix one component can unexpectedly affect another, and developers may find themselves adding increasingly specific selectors to override previous styles. Over time, these changes make CSS difficult to understand and update.

CSS cascade layers provide a way to organize styles into named groups and control their priority. Instead of relying entirely on selector specificity and the order of declarations, developers can establish a predictable structure for their stylesheets.

CSS determines which declarations apply by considering factors such as origin, importance, cascade layer priority, specificity, and source order. When several rules target the same element, understanding these factors helps explain why one style overrides another.

If all three rules apply to the same button under normal author styles, the ID selector wins because it has greater specificity.

This can become inconvenient when a project contains third-party styles, reusable components, and application-specific overrides. Developers may respond by adding more specific selectors, making future changes increasingly difficult.

Cascade layers offer another approach: establish a clear priority order before writing individual component rules.

A useful starting point is to divide styles according to their purpose. For example, a project might contain reset styles, third-party styles, reusable components, and page-specific adjustments.

You can establish these layers at the beginning of your stylesheet:

The declaration at the top establishes the order for normal declarations in these layers. For normal author styles, later layers have higher priority than earlier layers, regardless of selector specificity between those layers.

This means a simple selector in a higher-priority layer can override a more specific selector in a lower-priority layer.

For more background on building adaptable interfaces, developers can explore SitePoint's introduction to CSS container queries, which explains another way to structure maintainable component styles.

Not every project needs the same number of layers. A small website may require only a few, while a large application may benefit from a more detailed structure.

This is a suggested structure rather than a mandatory convention. The important part is defining the priority order intentionally and applying it consistently.

Cascade layers can help avoid selectors that become unnecessarily complicated.

For normal declarations, the second rule wins because overrides has higher layer priority, even though the first selector contains an ID and more class selectors.

This can make changes easier to review because developers do not need to keep increasing selector specificity to achieve the intended result.

However, layer order should not become an excuse to place every exception in a global override layer. Keep related styles close to their components and use overrides only when the exception is intentional.

Cascade layers have rules that developers need to understand before adopting them across an existing codebase.

For normal declarations, later layers have higher priority. For declarations marked !important, the layer priority is reversed. Important declarations in earlier layers take precedence over important declarations in later layers.

Unlayered normal author styles also take precedence over normal declarations inside author cascade layers. This matters when integrating a layered stylesheet with older CSS that remains outside the layer structure.

The MDN documentation on CSS cascade layers explains these priority rules and provides additional examples.

Before reorganizing a production stylesheet, test how existing third-party rules, inline styles, and important declarations interact with the new structure.

Rewriting an entire stylesheet at once can introduce regressions. A safer approach is to define the intended layer order, migrate one group of styles at a time, and compare the rendered interface after each change.

Start with styles that are easy to isolate, such as resets or a small set of reusable components. Check buttons, forms, navigation, and responsive layouts at several viewport sizes.

Browser developer tools can help identify which declaration is winning and whether it belongs to the expected layer. Visual regression tests are also useful when the application has many shared components.

For teams, documenting the layer order and agreeing on where new styles belong can prevent the stylesheet from becoming disorganized again.

CSS cascade layers provide developers with a practical way to manage style priority in growing applications. By separating resets, vendor styles, components, and utilities into a clear hierarchy, teams can reduce specificity conflicts and make stylesheets easier to maintain.

The best results come from a deliberate layer structure, consistent naming, and careful testing during migration. Cascade layers do not remove the need to understand CSS specificity, but they give developers another tool for controlling how styles interact.

#10374. Android 17 is on 1% of devices after four months, Android 16 on over 25%

Google has updated its Android distribution numbers with the latest update showing that Android 17 is on just 1% of devices, while Android 16 now makes up the biggest slice of the pie.

Updated as of October 19, Google’s latest Android distribution numbers offer a peek into the rollout speed of Android 17. Having released to Pixel phones in June, the update has been available for roughly four months.

At this point, though, Android 17 makes up just 1% of active Android devices, Google’s data shows.

That’s compared to over 25% for Android 16, which released last year. Android 16 was on 7.5% of devices in Google’s last update in December 2025/January 2026, which landed several months after Google released the update. The timing here requires context, as major players like Samsung have only started widely rolling out their Android 17 updates in the past few weeks and are very unlikely to be included in this 1%.

Fragmentation issues still plague Google's ability to control it's experiences. Seemingly no plans to address.

The growth of Android 16 is pretty impressive, too, as older versions tend to be still be more widely in use at this point in the schedule, but Android 16 has managed to consolidate quite a bit.

Google dropped Android 5 (Lollipop) from its data with this update, with Android 5.1 making up just 0.2% of active devices. Android 11, for reasons unclear, still holds over 10%, while Android 12 has dropped to 9.6%. Android 11 has had a higher share in the past few updates.

#10373. AI uncovers hidden Ozempic side effects across 400,000 Reddit posts

Artificial intelligence is giving researchers a new way to listen to what patients are saying about popular GLP-1 drugs. After analyzing more than 400,000 Reddit posts, a University of Pennsylvania team identified several symptoms reported by people using semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro and Zepbound) that may not be fully represented in clinical trials or official regulatory information.

The study, published recently in Nature Health, examined more than five years of posts from nearly 70,000 Reddit users. Two categories stood out as particularly deserving of further investigation: reproductive symptoms, including changes in menstrual cycles, and problems involving body temperature, such as chills and hot flashes.

The findings do not establish that the medications caused these symptoms. Instead, researchers say the massive collection of spontaneous patient reports may reveal signals worth examining more closely.

"Some of the side effects we found, like nausea, are well known, and that shows that the method is picking up a real signal," says Sharath Chandra Guntuku, Research Associate Professor in Computer and Information Science (CIS) at Penn Engineering and the study's senior author. "The underreported symptoms are leads that came from patients themselves, unprompted, and clinicians could potentially pay attention to them."

What Patients Report Outside Clinical Trials

Clinical trials are designed to determine whether treatments work and to identify important safety problems, but they cannot necessarily capture every symptom that matters to patients once a medication is being used by a much larger population.

"Clinical trials generally identify the most dangerous side effects of drugs," adds Lyle Ungar, Professor in CIS and a co-author on the study. "But they can fail to find what symptoms patients are most concerned about; even though social media is not necessarily representative, a large collection of posts may reflect additional concerns."

The distinction is important. The study found associations in what people discussed online, not proof that GLP-1 drugs were responsible for those experiences.

"We can't say that GLP-1s are actually causing these symptoms," notes Neil Sehgal, the study's first author and a doctoral student in CIS advised by Guntuku and Ungar. "But nearly 4% of the Reddit users in our sample reported menstrual irregularities, which would be even higher in a female-only sample. We think that's a signal worth investigating."

Using Social Media as an Early Health Signal

The idea of mining online conversations for clues about drug safety predates today's AI boom. In 2011, Ungar participated in one of the earliest efforts to use material created by internet users to identify possible adverse effects from medications.

Social media can capture experiences that patients discuss with one another but may never formally report to a doctor, drug manufacturer, or regulator.

"Online patient communities work a lot like a neighborhood grapevine," says Ungar. "People who are living with these medications are swapping notes with each other in real time, sharing experiences that rarely make it into a doctor's office visit or an official report."

Since then, online patient communities have expanded enormously. That has made social media a potentially valuable source for studying how medications affect people in everyday life, although gaining access to platform data has become more difficult.

Traditional clinical research remains essential, the researchers emphasize, but online conversations can provide information far more quickly when millions of people begin using a drug.

"Clinical trials are the gold standard, but by design, they are slow," says Guntuku. "This is not a replacement for trials, but it can move much faster, and that speed matters when a drug goes from niche to mainstream almost overnight."

AI Makes Massive Social Media Analysis Possible

One of the biggest obstacles has always been scale.

Guntuku describes the approach as "computational social listening," which uses computational methods to identify patterns in large collections of online conversations about health.

Patients, however, rarely describe symptoms using standardized medical terminology. One person might describe feeling unusually cold, another might mention constant chills, while a clinician could categorize those experiences using a specific medical term.

Researchers therefore need a way to translate everyday language into standardized categories. One important reference is the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA), which provides terminology widely used to classify medical conditions, symptoms, and adverse events.

Previously, connecting huge numbers of informal social media posts with standardized medical terminology required enormous amounts of work, limiting how much data researchers could realistically analyze.

Large language models such as GPT and Gemini are changing that equation by allowing researchers to process and categorize vast amounts of text more consistently and quickly.

"Large language models have made it possible to do this kind of analysis much faster with a level of standardization that could be difficult to achieve before," says Sehgal.

Unexpected Symptoms Emerge From 400,000 Posts

The researchers stress that Reddit users do not represent the overall population of people taking GLP-1 drugs. Reddit users tend to be younger, are more likely to be male, and are disproportionately located in the United States.

Even with that limitation, the analysis produced a reassuring sign that the approach was detecting genuine patterns. Many of the symptoms discussed by Reddit users closely matched already known effects of semaglutide and tirzepatide.

About 44% of users included in the study described at least one side effect. Gastrointestinal problems were the most common, consistent with the nausea and other digestive issues already associated with these medications.

More intriguing were symptoms that appeared frequently enough to attract the researchers' attention but may not be as well represented in current drug labels or conventional adverse event reports.

Nearly 4% of users who reported side effects described reproductive symptoms. These included changes in menstruation such as bleeding between periods, heavy bleeding, and irregular menstrual cycles.

Users also described changes involving body temperature, including chills, feeling unusually cold, hot flashes, and symptoms resembling a fever.

Fatigue was another notable finding. It was the second most frequently reported complaint in the Reddit data, even though relatively few clinical trials reported fatigue often enough for it to reach established reporting thresholds.

Why Menstrual and Temperature Changes Are Interesting

One possible reason these reports caught researchers' attention involves the hypothalamus, a small but extremely important region of the brain. Among its many jobs, the hypothalamus helps regulate hunger, hormones, reproduction and body temperature.

"These drugs are thought to work by engaging part of the brain called the hypothalamus, which helps regulate a wide variety of hormones," says Jena Shaw Tronieri, Senior Research Investigator at Penn's Center for Weight and Eating Disorders and a co-author of the study. "That doesn't mean the medications are necessarily causing these symptoms, but it could suggest that reports of menstrual changes and body temperature fluctuations are worth studying more systematically."

The researchers are not proposing that this biological connection proves GLP-1 drugs are responsible. Instead, it offers another reason to test the patient-reported patterns more carefully through controlled research.

Turning Online Conversations Into Research Leads

For now, the team hopes the results encourage scientists and clinicians to pay closer attention to symptoms that patients repeatedly discuss online.

"They're clearly on patients' minds, and that's worth paying attention to," says Sehgal.

The researchers also want to broaden their analysis beyond Reddit and beyond English-language communities. Doing so could help determine whether the same patterns emerge among different groups of people and on different social media platforms.

"We don't really know yet whether what we're seeing on Reddit reflects the experience of GLP-1 users globally, or whether it's particular to the kind of person who posts on Reddit in the United States," Ungar says.

In the longer term, rapid AI analysis of online patient conversations could potentially become an early detection system for emerging health concerns involving drugs, supplements and wellness products.

That could be particularly valuable for substances that become popular online faster than conventional research can keep up. Loosely regulated or unregulated products, including injectable peptides, can spread quickly through communities on Reddit, TikTok and other platforms. Discussions among users may therefore provide some of the earliest indications of unexpected effects.

"The whole point of this kind of approach is that it can move quickly, and that's exactly when it's most valuable," says Guntuku.

This study was conducted at the University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science. The authors report no outside funding. Tronieri reports receiving an investigator-initiated grant, on behalf of the University of Pennsylvania, from Novo Nordisk and receiving consulting fees from Currax Pharmaceuticals, LLC. The other authors report no conflicts of interest.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has met with about 50 senior Samsung executives in South Korea, as the company seeks to expand its Artificial Intelligence and memory capacity, Bloomberg reports. Altman’s visit to South Korea follows his recent comments about how the world's limited memory supply should be allocated. In an interview on the Chick Pink podcast this week, the OpenAI chief argued that DRAM sitting inside personal computers is often underused, describing it as “quite terrible”. He suggested that data centers could make more intensive use of memory by sharing computer resources across AI workloads. The argument has drawn widespread criticism given OpenAI’s own services like ChatGPT rely heavily on centralized computing infrastructure.

The meeting, which took place at Samsung’s Resources Development Center in Yongin on Saturday, October 30, brought together chiefs from the company’s financial, electronics, and biotechnology businesses. Confirming the meeting, Samsung Korea said the discussion revolved around strengthening existing relationships between the two companies, particularly a letter of Intent signed in October 20225 to cooperate on global AI infrastructure, including supplying memory semiconductors for OpenAI’s Stargate project. “The Samsung executives and CEO Sam Altman discussed the direction of AI technology development and its potential applications, as well as new markets and business opportunities that will emerge from it,” Samsung stated.

Samsung, however, emphasized more on AI transformation and future business opportunities, rather than announcing a new memory supply agreement. Reportedly, Altman also presented Samsung’s AI Center head with a Codex Micro Keyboard, a device designed for use with OpenAI’s coding agent. The latest meeting comes as demand from AI centers continues to soar, with AMD forecasting DRAM revenue will jump 177% in 2026 to about $416 billion. Trendforce also estimates DRAM supply will fall 1% to 2% short of demand this year, with the imbalance expected to worsen in 2027. New manufacturing capacity may take time to come, which means the shortage could persist into 2028, as per a recent warning by Micron.

For now, demand for data centers is facing major competition, especially from PCs, smartphones, and other electronics, for limited memory supplies (and may be nowhere close to peaking). High-bandwidth memory (HBM), a specialized form of DRAM used in AI devices, has become particularly important as companies deploy increasingly powerful computing systems.

Samsung and SK Hynix are among the world's leading memory manufacturers, giving South Korea a central role in supplying the hardware behind the AI expansion. According to Counterpoint Research, both companies controlled about 63% of global DRAM revenues in the second quarter of 2026. Their influence is greater in HBM, where the two South Korean manufacturers accounted for roughly 83% of global revenue. This has prompted other technology executives to approach the country, with AMD CEO Lisa Su visiting earlier this month to discuss securing additional HBM supplies from SAMSUNG, saying, "It is important to plan three to five years ahead with our partners."

Meanwhile, Samsung and SK Hynix have been upgrading Chinese factories to meet the surging demand for AI-related memory and storage products. However, those particular upgrades concern NAND flash production, rather than DRAM — but they show just how manufacturers are adjusting capacity as demand shifts towards data center hardware.

#10369. The shape behind the Einstein problem just revealed strange new physics

A mathematical shape that drew global attention for solving a decades-old puzzle is now revealing an unexpected connection to physics. Researchers have found that structures based on the shape can make light form unusual chiral patterns, pointing to new ways of exploring how geometry can influence optical behavior.

In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and collaborating institutions built optical structures inspired by the "Smith hat." This unusual shape is known for solving the so-called Einstein problem in mathematics. When the team illuminated the structures with laser light, they observed diffraction effects unlike those seen in conventional quasicrystals.

The Shape That Solved the Einstein Problem

The Einstein problem asks whether a single tile shape, known as a "monotile," can cover an entire surface without creating a repeating pattern.

Familiar tilings such as checkerboards and honeycombs repeat in a regular way. An aperiodic monotile, by contrast, can fill a surface without ever settling into a repeating arrangement.

In 2023, researchers discovered the first such monotile, the Smith hat. The finding attracted widespread attention because it provided a long-sought solution to the mathematical problem.

"What is especially fascinating about the hat tile is that, although the resulting pattern appears irregular at first glance, it is actually constructed from the honeycomb lattice," says lead author Yuto Moritake. "We wanted to see whether this unique shape could also produce any unexpected physical phenomena."

Turning a Mathematical Pattern Into an Optical Structure

To test that possibility, the researchers created nanoscale versions of the pattern on silicon nitride films using electron beam lithography.

When laser light was directed at the structures, the resulting diffraction patterns formed distinctive pinwheel-like shapes. These patterns directly revealed the chiral character of the aperiodic structure.

Chirality refers to a form of handedness in which a structure and its mirror image cannot be perfectly matched. In this case, the unusual arrangement of the monotile pattern caused the light itself to display a chiral response.

"We found that the diffraction patterns themselves become chiral because the structure lacks mirror symmetry," explains senior author Masaya Notomi. "This kind of optical response is fundamentally different from that observed in conventional quasicrystalline materials."

Light Responds to Direction and Polarization

The researchers also found that the diffraction pattern changed depending on both the direction and polarization of the incoming light.

When the physical structures were mirrored, their optical behavior reversed as well. This showed that the response of the light was directly tied to the symmetry of the underlying pattern, revealing a new type of symmetry-controlled optical behavior.

"These results open a new direction of research on the fusion of quasiperiodic order and chirality," remarks Moritake. "Monotile patterns provide a platform for exploring optical phenomena that emerge from the interplay of symmetry, chirality, and aperiodicity."

From Abstract Mathematics to New Optical Physics

The researchers say structures inspired by monotiles could eventually contribute to technologies designed to manipulate light, control polarization, and support advanced optical devices.

More broadly, the findings show how a discovery that began as an abstract mathematical puzzle can lead to unexpected physical effects. The Smith hat was first celebrated for solving a question about how shapes can cover a surface. Now, its unusual geometry may also help researchers uncover new ways to control and study light.

Materials provided by Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10366. MIT’s tiny flying robot gets 450% faster with AI

Tiny flying robots may one day help rescuers search for people trapped beneath collapsed buildings after earthquakes. Because of their small size, these robotic insects could potentially move through narrow spaces that larger drones cannot enter while avoiding walls, debris, and falling objects.

Until recently, however, aerial microrobots have been far less nimble than the insects that inspired them. They typically moved slowly and followed relatively simple flight paths.

Researchers at MIT have now demonstrated a new approach that gives an insect-scale flying robot much greater speed and agility. The team developed an AI-based controller that allows the robotic bug to perform demanding aerial maneuvers, including repeated body flips.

Using a two-part control system designed to balance performance with computational efficiency, the researchers increased the robot's speed by about 450 percent and its acceleration by about 250 percent compared with their previous best results.

The robot was agile enough to complete 10 consecutive somersaults in 11 seconds, even while wind disturbances tried to knock it away from its intended path.

"We want to be able to use these robots in scenarios that more traditional quadcopter robots would have trouble flying into, but that insects could navigate. Now, with our bioinspired control framework, the flight performance of our robot is comparable to insects in terms of speed, acceleration, and the pitching angle. This is quite an exciting step toward that future goal," says Kevin Chen, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), head of the Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory within the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), and co-senior author of a paper on the robot.

Chen is joined on the paper by co-lead authors Yi-Hsuan Hsiao, an EECS MIT graduate student; Andrea Tagliabue PhD '24; and Owen Matteson, a graduate student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AeroAstro); as well as EECS graduate student Suhan Kim; Tong Zhao MEng '23; and co-senior author Jonathan P. How, the Ford Professor of Engineering in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). The research was published in Science Advances.

AI Gives the Robot a Smarter Flight Controller

Chen's group has spent more than five years developing robotic insects.

The team recently created a more durable version of their tiny robot, which is about the size of a microcassette and weighs less than a paperclip. This newer design has larger flapping wings that support more agile flight. The wings are driven by soft artificial muscles that contract rapidly enough to produce extremely fast wingbeats.

The physical design had improved, but the robot's controller remained a major limitation. This controller acts as the robot's "brain," determining where the robot is and deciding how it should move. In earlier versions, a human had to tune the controller by hand.

For the robot to fly with the speed and aggressiveness of a real insect, the researchers needed a system that could handle uncertainty while rapidly solving complex control problems.

A controller powerful enough to do that would normally demand too much computation to operate in real time, especially because the aerodynamics of such a lightweight flying machine are highly complex.

To solve this problem, Chen's group collaborated with How's team to develop a two-step AI-driven control system. The design combines the robustness needed for difficult, high-speed maneuvers with enough computational efficiency to work in real time.

"The hardware advances pushed the controller so there was more we could do on the software side, but at the same time, as the controller developed, there was more they could do with the hardware. As Kevin's team demonstrates new capabilities, we demonstrate that we can utilize them," How says.

Teaching a Tiny Robot to Plan Difficult Maneuvers

The first part of the system uses what is known as a model-predictive controller. This type of controller relies on a dynamic mathematical model to predict how the robot will behave and determine the best sequence of actions for safely following a desired flight path.

Although this method requires substantial computing power, it can plan difficult movements such as aerial flips, sharp turns, and aggressive changes in body angle. The planner also takes into account limits on the amount of force and torque the robot can produce, helping it avoid movements that could lead to a crash.

Repeated flips are particularly challenging. To perform one somersault after another, the robot must slow down in exactly the right way so that it begins each new flip under the proper conditions.

"If small errors creep in, and you try to repeat that flip 10 times with those small errors, the robot will just crash. We need to have robust flight control," How says.

The researchers then used this expert planner to train a "policy" built on a deep-learning model through a process called imitation learning. The policy serves as the robot's real-time decision-making system, determining how and where it should fly.

In effect, imitation learning allows the team to capture the behavior of the more computationally demanding controller in a faster AI model that can operate quickly enough for real-time flight.

A major part of the challenge was generating enough useful training data to teach the policy how to handle aggressive maneuvers without creating an unnecessarily large data set.

"The robust training method is the secret sauce of this technique," How explains.

During flight, the AI-based policy receives information about the robot's position and converts it into real-time commands controlling factors such as thrust force and torques.

Experiments showed that the two-step control system dramatically improved the robot's performance. The insect-scale machine flew 447 percent faster and achieved a 255 percent increase in acceleration.

It also completed 10 somersaults in only 11 seconds while remaining within about 4 or 5 centimeters of its planned flight path.

"This work demonstrates that soft and microrobots, traditionally limited in speed, can now leverage advanced control algorithms to achieve agility approaching that of natural insects and larger robots, opening up new opportunities for multimodal locomotion," says Hsiao.

The team also demonstrated a movement known as a saccade. In insects, this involves pitching the body sharply, rapidly moving to a new position, and then pitching in the opposite direction to stop. This quick acceleration and braking can help insects determine their position and maintain clear vision.

"This bio-mimicking flight behavior could help us in the future when we start putting cameras and sensors on board the robot," Chen says.

One major goal for future research is to equip the microrobots with onboard cameras and sensors. That could eventually allow them to fly outdoors without depending on a sophisticated external motion capture system.

The team also plans to investigate whether onboard sensing could help groups of the robots avoid crashing into one another and coordinate their movements while navigating.

"For the micro-robotics community, I hope this paper signals a paradigm shift by showing that we can develop a new control architecture that is high-performing and efficient at the same time," says Chen.

This research is funded, in part, by the National Science Foundation (NSF), the Office of Naval Research, Air Force Office of Scientific Research, MathWorks, and the Zakhartchenko Fellowship.
